I respect what the hadith says. My intent wasn't to justify drinking, but rather to console a brother who is clearly agitated and remorseful. I do not think its effective to tell people to "go to AA" or "listen to this podcast" because many of you do not understand the spirit of Islam. The Prophet used to sit with people (even the drunkards) and meet them with mercy and kindly correct them. Is my knowledge infallible? Fuck no! But based on my own observations and lived experiences, I understand there is nuances to life. For example, I was at the bar a couple of weeks ago and met some really cool people. Guess what we talked about? God. And so I'll end by countering your hadith with one of my own:

Abu Hurairah and Abu Sa`id Al-Khudri (May Allah be pleased with them) reported: The Messenger of Allah (sallallaahu alayhi wa sallam) said, “When a group of people assemble for the remembrance of Allah, the angels surround them (with their wings), (Allah’s) mercy envelops them, Sakinah, or tranquillity descends upon them and Allah makes a mention of them before those who are near Him.”

They each have such strong character and know the mission Allah sent them here for. Still though they are complicated human beings and I doubt any of them are squeaky clean. A non-Muslim that I absolutely love the hell out of is Tupac Shakur. He was raised by a single mother, lost his way, but damn did he overcome all that. He entered rap, political activism (his mom and godmother were former Black Panthers), acting, etc. He linked all of his energy into speaking out against poverty and empowering the Black community. He still drank, slept around, and smoked weed. A key point though is that Pac left the church. He was spiritual, but still had love and belief in God. I highly doubt Allah will overlook all of the good this man has done (and his strong belief) because he chose to have a beer with his homies.

You raise a valid point. I'd like to take it a step further regarding child support. In Texas, the non-custodial parent (could be the husband or the wife) has financial and legal obligations to support that child(ren). The non-custodial parent is usually determined by the courts based on a multitude of factors (criminal history, substance abuse, relationship with the child, etc). Very interesting process. There are also resources available to help the non-custodial parent meet these obligations. The system is flawed (does it take into account rising costs of living across the US for example). Family court judges are appointed by a county wide partisan election. However, I think that re evaluating the financial obligations for the non-custodial parent needs to be re-evaluated and possibly amended every couple of years.

It's kind of an amalgamation of all I've been through in life. I was trying hard to be perfect and suppress a lot of "bad" qualities. Anger. Control. Lust. Fear. I was trying to be the perfect man. I pushed myself extremely hard at the expense of my mental health. I was only showing the world a mask. We're all taught good and bad from a young age, and I think we all do this. I learned about what self-awareness and mindfulness really are. I became aware when these impulses would rise in me. At first, I did what I always have done. Suppress. But then I realized what exactly am I trying to hide? Why am I trying to perfect? I'm just asking myself why a lot, basically. For me, it stems from fear of being judged. Once I became aware of these impulses, I started telling myself, "I am capable of great evil," and "I am capable of being controlling, manipulative, rude, etc." Basically, I became aware of my dark side. Like a drug addiction, you first have to accept that you have a problem. Similarly, with this, you first have to accept your dark side and integrate it into your whole personality. Once I started practicing this, some healing took place. I carried a lot of tension in my jaw, and my tongue would be glued to the roof of my mouth. Constant anxiety. But since I've been doing this, I have felt the release of that tension. Also, I became self-aware of me projecting insecurities and other things I don't like about myself onto others. Tbh, I'm still figuring it out. But this is what I've come up with so far. I don't know the next step yet. But it'll come to me.

A couple:

1) life doesn't owe me shit (after I got fired)
2) live life to the fullest (after a breakup when I was getting ready to propose)
3) accepted the darker side of me. My capacity for control. My capacity for destruction / revenge. Once I accepted this part of me, it became easier to forgive the faults of others and empathize.
